4 Ecosystems

4.1 The Sonoran Desert

Key words: adaptations · ecology · ecosystem · environment · food web · habitat · interact · nectar · nocturnal · pollen · pollinating

A desert in Arizona

Deserts are not easy places for animals and plants to live. Deserts do not get much rainfall, so the organisms that live there must have adaptations that help them to survive with little water.

The tall plants in the photograph are saguaro cacti. They grow very slowly, and some are more than 100 years old. Their roots spread out widely just underneath the soil, ready to absorb any rain that falls.

Many animals live among the cacti and other desert plants.

  • Gila woodpeckers make holes in the cacti to make their nests. Other birds also visit these holes.
  • Cactus wrens nest in a different kind of cactus, the teddy bear cholla. It is so spiky that very few other animals will get close to it, so the wren's eggs and young are protected from predators.

During the hot days, lizards, tortoises and other animals rest in the shade of the plants, or burrow into the soil where it is cooler. At night, when the temperature falls, kangaroo rats come out to feed, wary of predators such as rattlesnakes and coyotes.

In the Sonoran Desert it usually rains heavily at least once a year. When the rains come, the desert is transformed. Many plants quickly produce flowers. Insects feed on the nectar and pollen in the flowers, pollinating them and helping the plants to reproduce. At night, bats feed on nectar from the flowers of agave plants.

Seeds fall to the ground and are collected by ants, to take into their nests as a food store. Many months or years later, some of the uneaten seeds may germinate to produce new plants.

Interactions in the Sonoran Desert

All the different animals and plants in the desert depend on each other. They interact with each other: the actions of one organism affect another.

Non-living things in the desert

It is not only other organisms that affect the plants and animals. There are also interactions between the organisms and the non-living parts of their environment.

Non-living factorHow it affects the organisms
LightBright sunlight helps the plants to photosynthesise, producing food that other organisms can eat.
TemperatureOften very high by day but much lower at night. Some animals are nocturnal, which helps them avoid overheating or drying out.
SoilRocks and soil provide minerals for plants to grow, and building material for ground-nesting birds. It is cooler under the soil, so some animals dig burrows for shelter during the day.
WaterAll organisms need water to keep their cells alive. Rain, when it comes, allows them to become more active and to reproduce.
AirThe desert air provides carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and oxygen for all the organisms to use in respiration.

The organisms also affect their environment. For example, droppings from the kangaroo rats become part of the soil, and the gases the animals take in and give out affect the composition of the air.

The desert ecosystem

Everything in the desert interacts with everything else. All of these interactions make up the desert ecosystem.

Remember: an ecosystem is a network of interactions between all the living organisms and the non-living things around them.

Some of the interactions in an ecosystem involve food webs. Plants are the producers in a food web — they use energy in sunlight to make food. As animals eat the desert plants and each other, the energy is passed through the food web.

Food webs are a very important part of the interactions in an ecosystem, but they are not the only ones. For example:

  • plants provide places for some animals to make nests
  • plant roots help to hold the soil together, so it is not washed away when it rains
  • animals help plants to reproduce by pollinating their flowers or spreading their seeds.

The interactions in an ecosystem are usually very complicated. The study of ecosystems is called ecology. No ecologist would ever claim to have discovered all of the different interactions in an ecosystem.

Habitats in a desert ecosystem

The place where an organism naturally lives is called its habitat. There are many different places to live in a desert.

OrganismHabitat
Saguaro cactusthe open desert
Gila woodpeckera saguaro cactus (nest), and the air and ground in the open desert (food)
Desert antunderneath rocks and soil, and on the soil surface
Termitethe base of the saguaro stems
Sap beetleinside the saguaro flowers
Kangaroo ratburrows, coming out to look for food at night
Remember: a habitat is a place where an organism lives. An ecosystem is the whole network of interactions between the organisms and their non-living surroundings. One ecosystem contains many habitats.

4.2 Different ecosystems

Key words: ecosystem · habitat

More about ecosystems

The ecosystem in the Sonoran Desert is just one of many different ecosystems on Earth. Here are three more examples.

Mangrove forest

  • Mangroves are trees that can grow with their roots in sea water. They form forests along the coasts of many tropical countries.
  • Young fish live among the mangrove roots, safe from larger fish that might eat them. Mud skippers climb out onto the mud when the tide is out, feeding on whatever they can find.
  • As the mangrove leaves fall onto the mud, they are decomposed by bacteria. Prawns and crabs eat the partly decomposed leaves.
  • Crab-eating macaques, a type of monkey, climb through the trees and catch crabs on the tree roots and mud.

Sea ice in the Arctic Ocean

  • During the winter in the Arctic Ocean, it is so cold that some of the sea water freezes.
  • Seals hunt for fish in the water, but have to come to the surface to breathe air.
  • Polar bears patrol the ice, looking for seals to kill and eat. Polar bears are good swimmers and can move from one ice floe to another.
  • Arctic foxes also look for food on the ice.
  • Enough light passes through the ice to allow tiny algae (single-celled plants) to grow on the underside of the ice floes. Tiny shrimp-like organisms eat the algae, and fish eat the shrimps.

Rice paddy

  • Not all ecosystems are natural. This area of rice paddies in Malaysia is farmed by people.
  • At some times of year the paddy fields are flooded with water. Algae grow in this shallow water, and on the mud at the sides of the flooded areas.
  • Fish swim into the flooded paddies from the irrigation canals. Frogs and dragonflies breed in the water.
  • Because the water is shallow, it heats up quickly during the day and cools down quickly at night.
  • Farmers often add fertiliser to the paddy fields. This makes not only the rice but also the algae grow faster, providing more food for the animals.
  • Many birds feed in and around the paddy fields.

Investigating a local ecosystem

You can study an ecosystem near your school — a garden area, part of a playing field, a group of trees or a pond.

ApparatusWhat it is used for
Pitfall trapA plastic cup set into the ground. Small animals that crawl or run over the surface, such as beetles, fall in and cannot get out. Check it regularly, or you may find just one extremely fat carnivorous beetle and nothing else.
Sweep netA large net on a long pole. Sweep it through long grass to catch insects, or use it in a pond or small stream.
Beating trayGently hit a branch with a stick while others hold a large sheet underneath, to find insects living in the lower branches of trees.
Hand lensLooking at very small organisms.
CameraPhotographing organisms you cannot name, so you can identify them later.
Keys and booksIdentifying the animals and plants that you find.

A good method is:

  1. Describe the ecosystem — how big it is, what plants grow there, whether it is light or shady, damp or dry.
  2. Find the different habitats in it, such as underneath stones, in the soil, on the soil surface, on leaves, in flowers, on tree trunks and in the air.
  3. List the organisms living in each habitat, and note what the animals are doing.
  4. If possible, visit at different times of day — or at night — to see how the ecosystem changes.
  5. Draw a diagram of the interactions you saw, between organisms and between organisms and the non-living parts of the environment.
Remember: if you catch any animals you must take great care of them. Do not take them away from their habitat — release them exactly where you found them.

4.3 Intruders in an ecosystem

Key words: eradicate · extinct · native species

New species in an ecosystem

All the organisms in an ecosystem interact with each other and with their environment. So what happens if a new species suddenly arrives? How does it fit into the network of interactions, and how does that affect the species already there?

A native species is a species that belongs naturally in that place. A species brought in from somewhere else is an introduced species. An introduced species that spreads and causes harm is called an invasive species.

Introduced species in New Zealand

New Zealand became separated from all the other areas of land in the world about 66 million years ago. Because of this separation, the species that developed there were different from those elsewhere on Earth.

Before humans arrived, there were no predatory mammals in New Zealand. Many of the native birds nest on the ground, because there were no predators to eat their eggs. Several native birds, such as the kiwi, cannot even fly.

Humans probably arrived about 700 years ago, and brought other species with them.

SpeciesWhy it arrivedWhat happened
RatsStowed away on boatsRats now live in most of the country. They eat birds' eggs and defenceless young birds.
SheepBrought by farmers for wool and meatFarmed in pastures.
RabbitsBrought on sailing ships as foodThey escaped and began to eat the grass in the sheep pastures.
StoatsBrought from Europe to control the rabbitsStoats spread all over New Zealand.

Stoats are fierce hunters and breed rapidly. They can kill and eat birds much larger than themselves. Stoats have made several species of native bird extinct, including the laughing owl and the New Zealand thrush, and they eat almost 60% of kiwi chicks.

People in New Zealand are now trying to eradicate stoats — that is, to get rid of them completely — but this is very difficult to do. The best that can be done is to control their numbers.

Scientists think that 53 species of native bird in New Zealand have become extinct since humans arrived. The extinctions were partly caused by people hunting the birds, but mostly by introduced invasive species.

Remember: a species is often harmless in its native ecosystem because predators, diseases and competitors keep its numbers down. In a new ecosystem those controls may be missing, so its numbers can grow very quickly.

Buffelgrass in the Sonoran Desert

Buffelgrass is native to Africa, Asia and the Middle East. It was planted in Arizona in the 1930s as food for cattle, and it is now spreading rapidly through the Sonoran Desert. It grows in dense patches and takes water and nutrients from the soil, so the native desert plants — including saguaro cacti — have less water and fewer nutrients. If the native plants suffer, so do the animals that depend on them.

4.4 Bioaccumulation

Key words: accumulate · bioaccumulation · biomagnification · insecticide · persistent · toxic

DDT

DDT is an insecticide. This means that it kills insects.

DDT was first produced in the 1940s. It was used to kill insects that transmit diseases — especially mosquitoes that transmit malaria, and fleas that transmit a disease called typhus. It was also used to kill insects that eat crops.

No one thought that DDT could harm organisms other than insects. But gradually people began to realise that it was also harming animals that no one wanted to kill. In 1962 an American author called Rachel Carson wrote a book called Silent Spring, describing how DDT was killing not only mosquitoes but also birds. Her book made many people realise that some insecticides are very harmful to the environment.

DDT in food chains

We now know that DDT does not break down. It is a persistent chemical:

  • it stays in the environment for many years
  • it is not broken down by decomposers
  • when it is sprayed, some of it is carried high into the air and can be blown very long distances, far away from where it was used
  • when it gets into an animal's body it stays there for the whole life of the organism.

DDT is toxic (poisonous) to many kinds of animal. For example, it makes the shells of birds' eggs very thin and easy to break.

Bioaccumulation and biomagnification

Imagine that DDT has been sprayed onto some water. Tiny protoctists take up some of the DDT. Shrimps eat the protoctists, fish eat the shrimps, and cormorants (fish-eating birds) eat the fish.

All the DDT in all of the protoctists that a shrimp eats over its lifetime accumulates, or builds up, in its body. The longer the organism lives, and the more DDT it takes in, the more DDT it gets in its body. This process is called bioaccumulation.

All of the DDT in all of the shrimps that a fish eats accumulates in the fish's body. Eventually, all the DDT in all of the fish that a cormorant eats in its lifetime accumulates in the cormorant's body.

This means that the concentration of DDT in an animal's body increases as you go up the food chain. This is called biomagnification.

The concentration is measured in parts per million (ppm). This is the number of grams of DDT in one million grams of the organism.

Part of the food chainConcentration of DDT / ppm
water0.000 05
protoctists0.04
shrimps0.16
minnows0.50
cormorants26.40
Remember: bioaccumulation is the build-up of a substance inside one organism over its lifetime. Biomagnification is the increase in concentration along a food chain, from one level to the next.

Biodegradable insecticides

Some insecticides are biodegradable, which means they can be broken down by microorganisms in the environment or inside an animal's body. A biodegradable insecticide does not stay in an animal's body for its whole life, so it does not build up along a food chain in the same way. Other substances that do not break down, such as microplastics, can build up in the environment in a similar way to DDT.

Summary checklist

  • I can describe some of the interactions between the organisms in a desert ecosystem.
  • I can describe some of the interactions between the organisms and the non-living parts of the environment in a desert ecosystem.
  • I can name some of the different habitats in a desert ecosystem.
  • I can explain the difference between a habitat and an ecosystem.
  • I can describe some of the habitats and interactions in other ecosystems, such as a mangrove forest, Arctic sea ice and a rice paddy.
  • I can use different methods to find out about habitats and interactions in an ecosystem near my school.
  • I can explain how new or invasive species can affect an ecosystem.
  • I can describe examples of invasive species and their effects.
  • I can explain what is meant by bioaccumulation.
  • I can explain why DDT shows bioaccumulation.
  • I can explain why organisms at the top of a food chain have higher concentrations of DDT in their bodies than organisms at the base of the food chain.
